strengths: Highly effective data-curation paradigm: Shifting from simple dataset scaling to sample complexity ($k$-value) is a very promising and well-motivated direction for visual instruction tuning (VIT).

Rigorous and fair comparison: The paper compares against a wide range of state-of-the-art data selection and pruning baselines (such as EL2N, SemDeDup, ICONS) under controlled environments, using the same base model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B) and training configurations.

Outstanding performance/efficiency trade-off: Achieves 100.2% of full LLaVA-665K performance using only 10% of the data budget, and significantly outperforms it on complex benchmarks such as MM-Vet (+8.6%) and MMStar (+2.9%).

Comprehensive analyses and ablations: The authors provide thorough analyses, including isolating the effects of the generator LLM by matching the baseline complexity distribution, evaluating with open-source VLMs (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct), and demonstrating high token efficiency (COMPACT uses 46.88% fewer tokens per entry).
weaknesses: Reliance on advanced VLMs for generation: The method relies heavily on high-performing closed-source models (like Gemini-2.0-Flash) or capable open-source models (like Qwen3-VL) to successfully generate and verify complex compositional questions, which could propagate the teacher's inherent biases or failure modes.

Complexity and cost of the generation pipeline: The multi-stage filtering has a non-negligible rejection rate (~21%), and verifying capability alignment via additional VLM prompt runs adds computational overhead and complexity to the dataset assembly pipeline.

strengths: Intuitive and well-motivated core idea: raising the density of visual information per question by explicitly composing atomic capabilities rather than just selecting or scaling simple questions.

Excellent data efficiency results, matching 100% of full LLaVA-665K performance with only 10% of the data budget (65K samples) and outperforming various state-of-the-art data pruning methods like ICONS and SemDeDup.

Thorough and convincing analysis, including a clever control experiment (COMPACT_llava matching the original distribution) to isolate the impact of sample complexity (k-value) from the generation source.
Broad and rigorous evaluation across 8 multimodal benchmarks, plus additional analyses on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, token efficiency, and ablations on the k-value ranges.
Great transparency and reproducibility with system prompts, quality analysis, cost details, and an open-source generator alternative (Qwen3).
weaknesses: The proposed dataset recipe relies on advanced proprietary VLMs (Gemini-2.0-Flash) for generation and dual-stage verification, which could introduce generation biases or cost barriers, although the authors successfully mitigate this concern by showing competitive results using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct.
The evaluation is primarily focused on LLaVA-1.5-7B. Testing on a more modern or different architecture/base LLM would further strengthen the generalizability claims of the COMPACT data recipe.

The choice of the 10 atomic capabilities is somewhat heuristic. While ablations show each capability contributes, a systematic exploration of how to automatically discover or scale these capabilities could make the framework more general.

strengths: Well-motivated and clean framework: Defining sample complexity ($k$-value) as the composition of fundamental atomic capabilities provides a structured way to analyze and curate visual instruction tuning datasets.

Superb data and training efficiency: By scaling complexity instead of dataset size, COMPACT achieves 100.2% of the full LLaVA-665K performance with only 10% of the dataset volume. Additionally, token-level analysis shows a ~47% reduction in total tokens processed, significantly cutting down fine-tuning costs.

Rigorous and transparent control experiments: The authors make a strong effort to isolate confounding variables, such as matching the complexity distribution using the same teacher model (Table 3) and testing an open-source alternative generator (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct in Table 9) to ensure robustness.

In-depth analysis and ablations: The paper provides highly informative insights, including the necessity of mixing simple and complex samples (Fig 4), identifying the optimal percentage of format-alignment instruction data (Fig 5), and assessing the contribution of individual capabilities (Table 7).
Excellent presentation: The writing is exceptionally clear, the figures are highly illustrative, and the appendices provide comprehensive details about the prompts and system statistics.
weaknesses: Teacher model confounding factor: The primary baselines (Table 2) use subsets of LLaVA-665K, which relied on older GPT-4/3.5 models. Since COMPACT leverages Gemini-2.0-Flash, a portion of the performance gain is likely due to the superior quality of the modern teacher model. While the authors mitigate this in Table 3 and Table 9, it remains an important factor in the main results.

Evaluation limited to LLaVA-1.5-7B: While LLaVA-1.5 is a standard research prototype for data selection/curation studies, evaluating on a more modern or larger MLLM architecture (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL) would further strengthen the generalizability of the proposed recipe.

Manual and heuristic taxonomy: The 10 atomic capabilities are predefined heuristically. It is unclear how this framework scales to highly specialized or non-visual tasks (e.g., complex math, multi-page document QA, or domain-specific reasoning) which fall outside the current set of atomic capabilities.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and persistent bottleneck in modern MLLMs: the lack of compositional complexity in visual instruction tuning (VIT) data, which leads to poor performance on multi-capability queries.
COMPACT demonstrates impressive data efficiency, achieving performance comparable to the full LLaVA-665K VIT dataset with only 10% of the data budget (65K total samples).

The proposed method uses a systematic taxonomy of 10 atomic capabilities and a robust four-step generation-and-verification pipeline with controlled complexity levels ($k$), ensuring high-quality and naturally integrated questions.
The model trained on COMPACT shows outstanding generalization to higher-order complexities ($k=4, 5$) on MM-Vet and MMStar, despite being trained only on $k \le 3$.

The paper is exceptionally well-written and includes thorough, insightful ablation studies, such as the leave-one-out capability analysis and the study of the optimal ratio between formatting and compositional data.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to LLaVA-v1.5-7B, which is somewhat dated. Validating the COMPACT recipe on a more recent and diverse set of MLLM architectures (e.g., Qwen2-VL or LLaVA-NeXT) would greatly strengthen the claim of its general applicability.

The data generation and verification pipeline heavily relies on a proprietary API (Gemini-2.0-Flash), which limits self-contained reproducibility and potentially inherits the internal biases of the proprietary model.
The paper lacks human evaluation to assess the actual semantic correctness and capability alignment ($k$) of the generated dataset.
There is a lack of direct comparison against other compositional data synthesis or augmentation baselines (e.g., Mosaic-IT).

strengths: Highly data-efficient: Achieves comparable performance to the full LLaVA-665K visual instruction tuning dataset using only 10% of the data budget (65K vs. 665K).

Systematic and balanced approach to compositionality: Directly addresses the 'complexity cliff' (where existing datasets are dominated by simple $k=1$ queries) by enforcing a balanced distribution across different levels of compositional complexity ($k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$).
Comprehensive evaluation: Evaluated across 8 diverse vision-language benchmarks, showing impressive zero-shot generalization to even higher-complexity tasks ($k \ge 4$).
Rigorous ablation and analysis: Includes a detailed leave-one-out capability analysis, validation of the complexity range, and exploration of the optimal ratio of standard instruction-tuning data.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The methodology relies heavily on prompt engineering and filtering using a commercial API (Gemini-2.0-Flash) rather than proposing a new model architecture or training objective.
Reliance on closed-source models: Utilizing commercial APIs for data generation and verification limits strict reproducibility, as the underlying models are subject to updates or deprecation.

Evaluation on slightly older baseline models: The experimental validation is primarily conducted on LLaVA-v1.5-7B. Testing the recipe on more recent open-source base models or advanced architectures would better demonstrate its modern-day relevance.

Limitations on knowledge-intensive tasks: As the authors note, the vision-centric atomic capabilities do not translate to significant improvements on benchmarks requiring substantial world knowledge (e.g., MMMU, OK-VQA).

strengths: The paper tackles a critical and timely challenge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): the lack of compositional reasoning capabilities resulting from simple, single-capability queries in traditional visual instruction tuning (VIT) datasets.
The proposed COMPACT data recipe is highly data-efficient, matching or exceeding the performance of the full LLaVA-665K dataset using only 10% of the training data budget.
Outstanding generalization performance is demonstrated on higher-complexity compositional queries (k=4 and k=5) even when the model is only trained on compositional complexity up to k=3.

The paper features exceptionally thorough and well-designed ablation studies, including a leave-one-out analysis of atomic capabilities, compositional complexity ranges, and the mixture ratio of instruction-following data.
weaknesses: The data generation and quality verification pipelines rely heavily on a closed-source proprietary model (Gemini-2.0-Flash), which limits independent reproducibility and introduces dependency risks.

The empirical evaluation is primarily restricted to the LLaVA-1.5-7B architecture trained with LoRA. Demonstrating the effectiveness of the COMPACT recipe on other modern MLLMs (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT or ShareGPT4V) would further validate its generalizability.

The paper lacks details regarding the concrete cost (e.g., API token usage or approximate monetary cost in USD) of generating the 32K compositional samples, which is important for researchers looking to reproduce or scale up the pipeline.
